KASPER

Act three. Enough background. Now we watch a platform decide, live, on a system small enough to run on this laptop.

Source: Ch 14.

KASPER

This is the book's blueprint for a governed agent platform, boiled down to nine pieces. Five of them are the building blocks the abstract promised: the agent runtime, the context layer, the tool gateway, policy and evals, and multi-agent over shared context. Tools, models and telemetry are what those blocks stand on.

Read it like this. A request goes from the agent runtime through the tool gateway to the tools and models. The gateway asks policy on every call that matters. The evidence goes the other way: telemetry, then evals. Each chip says how much Northstar shows. Gateway, policy and evals: shown, in depth. Runtime and telemetry: partial. Two blocks are missing: the context layer, meaning memory and retrieval, and multi-agent over shared context. Better you hear that now than in Q&A.

The row underneath is William's four rings, landed on it. Core, identity: SPIRE gives each agent a passport, and the gateway checks it. Ring 1, reach: Cilium, underneath the gateway, so the gateway is the only road to a tool. Ring 2, capability: the gateway and policy together. And the keystone: Kyverno, which stops an agent changing any of the other three.

IF ASKED 'why is the runtime only partial?' Because our agents can't run code. Their only way to change anything is an MCP call through the gateway, and the policy decides it. More advanced agents are different: a coding agent with a shell, a file system, a code interpreter. For those the next boundary is the runtime itself. Run the agent in an agent-sandbox Sandbox, the Kubernetes SIG project for exactly this, on a gVisor or Kata runtime class, so what the model writes and runs stays inside its own kernel boundary. Then let Kyverno refuse any agent pod without that runtime class, the same way the keystone protects authority today. Identity, reach and capability limit what an agent can call. A sandbox limits what it can execute.

[verify: kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox latest release and its SIG home before November]

Source: Ch 11 (Figure 11.1, section 11.2); M7 design spec §1 (the rings table).

KASPER

William said none of this is new. Here's what he meant. Read each row left to right. On the left, something your platform team already runs. On the right, the same idea pointed at agents. A golden path becomes a declared contract per agent. Admission policy becomes a decision at the tool gateway. Service identity becomes one SPIFFE identity per agent. Your observability stack learns GenAI traces and decision spans. A feature flag becomes the autonomy level, changed live. And the catalog becomes the view onto all of it. The last column is where each one lives in Northstar. So don't start an AI platform from scratch. Teach the one you have about agents.

Source: Ch 1 (Figure 1.8), Ch 11.

KASPER

So what makes a foundation governed, not just connected? Northstar comes up in seven stages, and each adds one thing you can prove. Read the stair left to right.

First, connected: the agents talk, and one trace covers the claim. That's plumbing. The second is the line: the platform starts deciding, and identity is an input to that decision. The second stage is where three of William's rings arrive at once: identity, reach and capability. Third: a human can overturn a refusal. Fourth: prove why money moved, from telemetry alone. Fifth: one live value changes what's allowed, no redeploy. That value is part of the capability ring. Sixth: Backstage is just the view.

And seventh, new: bounded. The agent can't edit what constrains it. That's the keystone, and its proof is a denial you'll watch live. The grey line under each stage is what it installs. Today we run the last one.

[verify: stage 7 (M7 Bounded) merged and gated before November. the five-minute flow (scripts/demo) has a captured live run, 2026-10-12.]

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §1 and §3 (Option 1); M7 design spec §1 and §2.1; Ch 4, Ch 11.

KASPER

Here is Northstar. A customer files claim CLM-1842. The claims agent checks it with plain rules, no model, and hands it on. The settlement agent is the only one with a model, Claude. To pay, it calls agentgateway, not the payment tool. The gateway checks who is calling, then asks the policy service, the box underneath, whether this payment is allowed. Only on a yes does it forward to payments-mcp and the ledger. Model calls go straight to Anthropic, not through the gateway. Cilium makes the gateway the only road to the tool. Everything reports to one Collector, at one hundred percent. Next: the rule behind this picture, then each tool.

[verify: pinned versions (agentgateway v1.6.0, Cilium 1.20.1, a2a-sdk 0.3.7) before November, Appendix B]

Source: Ch 4 (Figure 4.5).

KASPER

The design rule as a picture. Left: the model can request anything, even six thousand two hundred euros. Middle: one choke point the agent can't skip. Who is asking, and is it allowed? Right: only a permit becomes an effect. Why not limit the agent? An agent that can choose to ask permission can choose not to. The tool? That's an if-statement with extra steps. A test fails if one ever appears. So what fills that middle box? Here is every tool, by its job.

Source: Ch 4 (Figure 4.4, design principle 2), Ch 7 (Decision 2).

KASPER

Two words you'll hear from here on. An enforcement point stands at the door. Think of a bouncer. It lets a call through or stops it, and that's all it does. A decision point knows the rules. Think of the manager. The bouncer asks, the manager answers, and the manager never touches the door. In Northstar the bouncer is agentgateway, and the manager is our policy decision service. Keep them apart, and you can change the rule without touching the door.

Source: Ch 7; docs/architecture.md "The decision the platform makes".

KASPER

Every tool, grouped by the job it does. Read the top row first: the claim path. A2A is how agents talk to each other; MCP is how an agent calls a tool. Both now sit in the Agentic AI Foundation, under the Linux Foundation. Cilium, the network, makes the gateway the only road to the tool. SPIFFE and SPIRE give each agent pod a signed identity. agentgateway checks it and asks for a decision. The Policy Decision Service is our own code: permit or deny, and why. OpenFeature and flagd hold the autonomy level. Bottom row, around the path: the Collector takes every span, unsampled, to Jaeger, OpenSearch and Prometheus. Our eval-scorer writes scores back into the trace. Backstage is the view. The tinted chips mark code we wrote.

[verify: a2a-sdk 0.3.7, mcp 2.2.0, Cilium 1.20.1, SPIRE 1.15.3, agentgateway v1.6.0, Open Feature Operator v0.9.3, flagd v0.16.2, Collector contrib 0.160.0, Jaeger 2.20.0, OpenSearch 3.8.0, Prometheus v3.14.0, Backstage 1.54.0; OpenSearch's home is the OpenSearch Software Foundation under the LF; A2A joined AAIF 2026-08-17; OpenFeature still CNCF Incubating]

Source: docs/architecture.md (the two components tables); deploy/*; Ch 2 (Figure 2.12).

KASPER

The first ring, the core: identity. Who is this agent? In the platform world that's called workload identity. A name tag says who you claim to be. A passport is issued by someone else, checked at the border, and valid for one destination. SPIFFE is the standard for the name. SPIRE is the passport office. Follow the steps left to right. First: a ClusterSPIFFEID says which pods get which ID, and the controller-manager turns it into a registration. Second: the CSI driver mounts SPIRE's Workload API socket into the settlement-agent pod. Third: when the agent asks, the SPIRE agent checks the pod's namespace and ServiceAccount. Fourth: SPIRE issues a JWT-SVID for one audience, the gateway. Fifth: the gateway checks the signature against keys the OIDC discovery provider publishes, and writes jwt.sub on its span. Trust domain: northstar.local. One thing SPIRE does not do is emit spans. Metrics only.

[verify: SPIRE 1.15.3 still has no OTLP or tracing support]

Source: deploy/platform/spire/registration.yaml and values.yaml; agents/settlement-agent/svid.py; docs/architecture.md "Workload identity"; Ch 7.

KASPER

The next ring out is capability: what the agent may do. Most of that ring lives in the gateway. Before its config, what kind of thing is agentgateway?

Look left first. An ordinary API gateway sees an HTTP request: a POST to slash mcp, a host, a token. The body is just bytes to it. So it can make rules about URLs.

Now the right. agentgateway speaks the agent protocols. It opens the message and sees a tools/call, for the tool execute_payment, for six thousand two hundred euros, from settlement-agent. So it can make rules about the tool call itself. Think of a post office that only reads the envelope, next to a customs officer who opens the parcel.

Along the bottom: one proxy for three kinds of traffic. MCP, agent to tool. A2A, agent to agent. And LLM, agent to model. In our demo it guards one road: the MCP road to the payments tool. And Cilium makes sure it's the only road.

[verify: agentgateway v1.6.0 feature set: MCP, A2A and LLM routes; still LF/AAIF]

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml (one mcp backend, payments-mcp); tools/payments-mcp/server.py; docs/architecture.md "Hop 3".

KASPER

Still ring two, capability. Now the gateway's config. agentgateway is written in Rust, and it's a Linux Foundation project, in the Agentic AI Foundation, not CNCF. Our whole setup is one YAML file. Read it left to right: every tool call passes three checks, in this order. First, jwtAuth: who is asking? A bad or missing token gets HTTP 401 before the gateway even reads the MCP message. Second, mcpGuardrails: is it allowed? The gateway sends the call over gRPC to the policy service, and waits. failClosed means: if the policy service can't answer, the answer is no. A deny stops right here. Third: on a permit, the gateway drops the token and forwards. The tool never sees the agent's credential. Underneath, every step writes a span. You'll see them in a minute.

[verify: agentgateway v1.6.0 still the latest stable before November]

Source: deploy/platform/agentgateway/config.yaml; docs/architecture.md "Hop 3"; Ch 6, Ch 7.

KASPER

Still ring two. How much an agent may do also depends on a live setting, its autonomy level. That setting uses OpenFeature, so here's what that is.

OpenFeature is a CNCF standard for asking about feature flags. The question is standard. What answers it is pluggable. Think of a wall socket: every appliance fits the same socket, whatever power station is behind it.

Read the stack from the top. Our policy service asks one question: what is the autonomy level, for this SPIFFE ID? The OpenFeature SDK is the same API in every language, and it has hooks. We use the OpenTelemetry hook. Under it, a provider plugs in a backend. Ours is flagd, over gRPC on localhost. And the flag itself lives in a FeatureFlag, a Kubernetes object. The OpenFeature Operator puts the flagd sidecar in the pod for us.

Now the right: why use a flag for a policy knob? It changes without a deploy. The change is a one-word diff you can review. It's answered per caller. And every evaluation leaves evidence.

[verify: OpenFeature still CNCF Incubating; Open Feature Operator v0.9.3, flagd v0.16.2, openfeature-sdk 0.10.0 (Python)]

Source: platform/policy-decision-service/pds/autonomy.py and requirements.txt; deploy/platform/openfeature/featureflag.yaml and featureflagsource.yaml; deploy/k8s/policy-decision-service.yaml (openfeature.dev annotations).

KASPER

And this is the manager, the policy decision service, our own code. Read the right side first: the rule table. It has two keys: who is calling, and the autonomy level. settlement-agent at assisted may execute nothing: its limit is zero euros. At autonomous, up to six thousand. Above its limit a human decides, and that human is a different caller, the reviewer-ui. Any other caller has no row, and no row means deny. Now the left: where the level comes from. The FeatureFlag you just met, read through the flagd sidecar. If flagd can't answer, the level falls back to assisted. Every answer becomes a northstar.policy.decision span. The other key, identity, comes back after the demo. Keep one question in your head: if one value on one object decides this much, who is allowed to change that value? We answer it live, in step 4.

Source: platform/policy-decision-service/pds/rules.py and pds/autonomy.py; deploy/platform/openfeature/featureflag.yaml; docs/architecture.md (flagd row); Ch 7, Ch 8.

KASPER

SAY: "Here's the demo. Five steps, about five minutes. A customer files a vehicle-damage claim, our agents prepare the payment, and the platform decides who may release it. Each command lands one ring of what you've just seen."

THE SLIDE STAYS UP FOR THE WHOLE DEMO. It shows no commands: everything below is for you. Switch to the terminal and the two browser tabs; come back to the deck for "What you just saw".

———

Step 1 · live · terminal. Core · Identity and Ring 1 · Reach.

Plain words first: three ways to try to reach the payment tool. With no identity. Around the gateway. And with the agent's own identity.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo guard. No model. About nine seconds, eight of them waiting on purpose.
2. SHOW part 1, no identity: tools/list, then tools/call execute_payment, to the gateway with no token. Both HTTP 401, nothing forwarded.
SAY: "No identity, no conversation."
3. SHOW part 2, around the gateway, from inside claims-agent, a real pod with no SVID. First the control: settlement-agent on port 9002 answers 200, so the network works. Then an MCP initialize straight at payments-mcp: DROPPED.
SAY, during the 8-second wait: "That wait is the drop. There's no error to read, because nothing answered. The network threw the packet away. And notice: no span either. Cilium's drops are not in our trace, because Hubble, its flow viewer, isn't installed. This terminal line is the evidence."
4. SHOW part 3, with settlement-agent's identity: SPIRE mints the same token the agent holds (it's never printed), and tools/list through the gateway answers 200 with all four tools, including execute_payment, the one that moves money.
SAY: "Seeing a tool is not being allowed to use it. Listed is not permitted: every call is decided, one by one. That's the next step."

IF IT FAILS: "FAIL … the control did not answer" means the network is down, not the policy. "FAIL … was not dropped" means the Cilium policy isn't enforcing. No SPIRE token: the spire-server pod. In every case, say so and move on: the next slide shows what you meant to show.

[verify: Cilium 1.20.1, SPIRE 1.15.3 and agentgateway v1.6.0 still the pinned versions]

———

Step 2 · live · browser, then terminal. Ring 2 · Capability. A human signs.

Plain words first: the agent can do the work, but above its limit a person has to sign. This step shows that person.

1. DO: in the customer tab, file a claim for 5,800 euros. A real claim, through claims-agent, settlement-agent and the model. About seven seconds.
2. SHOW the customer tab: "Awaiting human approval", and a timer that keeps running. Nothing was paid.
SAY, while the model works: "The model decides what to propose. The platform decides what happens."
3. DO: switch to the reviewer tab. SHOW four facts: the rule, assisted; the limit, zero euros; the amount; and the model's own words. Read the narrative aloud: it says it needs a colleague to sign. It is telling the truth, because the platform told it the truth.
SAY: "This is maker-checker. The agent is the maker. It proposed the payment and tried to release it. The reviewer is the checker, a different service with a different identity. The agent can't approve its own payment, because the platform reads the ledger before it lets anyone release money."
4. DO: press Approve. SHOW: the customer tab flips to Settled, without a reload.
SAY: "The agent did the work. A human signed. The trace shows how long the human took."

About the trace on stage. Nothing polls while a claim waits: the claim's first trace ends at the hand-off. The approval starts a second trace, with a span link back to the first. Open either one in Jaeger at any time.

The no itself: HTTP 200. The gateway's answer is a tool result marked isError, with the rule in its text. A no is a decision, not an HTTP failure.

IF THE BROWSER MISBEHAVES: the terminal does both halves. ./scripts/demo claim 5800, then ./scripts/demo approve last. Then carry on.
IF THE CUSTOMER TAB NEVER FLIPS: finish with ./scripts/demo approve last. The payment is settled either way; only the tab is stale.

———

Step 3 · live · terminal. One live dial.

Plain words first: how much the agent may do is one value on one Kubernetes object, a FeatureFlag. flagd serves it, and the decision service reads it on every call.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo autonomy autonomous. Under a second. SHOW: flagd resolves autonomous, and "Pods restarted: NONE": twelve pods compared by UID, start time and restart count, before and after.
SAY: "I changed one value, from the command line. Nothing was redeployed, and the command counts the pods to prove it."
2. DO: ./scripts/demo claim 5800. The same amount you just saw wait. About seven seconds, then a short pause while the spans land. Fill it: "Same amount, same agent, same code, same image."
3. SHOW: SETTLED, by the agent. northstar.policy.decision permit, under a different rule, settlement-agent.autonomous.execute_limit, limit 6,000. The execute span is PRESENT: money moved, and no human was asked.
4. DO: ./scripts/demo claim 6200. SHOW: WAITING. The limit is 6,000, the request is 6,200, so the platform sends it to a human again.
SAY: "One live dial. The band widens; the human stays. More autonomy did not remove the human. It moved the line."
5. DO: ./scripts/demo autonomy assisted. SHOW assisted, and Pods restarted: NONE again. SAY: "And back."

The 6,200 claim is left waiting on purpose. ./scripts/demo reset ends it at the end of the talk.

The slide is the diff the first command makes: the first branch of the flag's targeting rule, assisted to autonomous.

HAZARD: never leave the flag at autonomous; the next run assumes assisted. ./scripts/demo reset fixes it. "FAIL … something restarted" means a rollout overlapped the flip: believe it and check the pods.
Worth knowing: the CLI flip leaves no audit span. Backstage's card writes the same value and records a northstar.autonomy_contract.change span; that's the optional slide after the demo.

———

Step 4 · live · terminal. The keystone.

Step 3 just showed that one value on one object changes what the agent may do. So who may change that value? If the answer is "the agent", every limit you've seen is a suggestion.

Plain words first. Kubernetes checks this change twice. RBAC, role-based access control, is the key card: which identity may touch which kind of object. Kyverno is an admission policy: a guard who reads each change before it's saved, and can say no even when your key card works.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo keystone. Half a second; talk over the output. It acts as the settlement agent's own Kubernetes identity.
2. SHOW the first row: the agent patches its own flag to autonomous. Forbidden, from RBAC: it "cannot get resource featureflags". Why get, when it asked to patch? kubectl reads the object before it patches it, and the agent may not even read it.
SAY: "RBAC says no. That's the first line."
3. SHOW the second row: the over-grant, a Role and RoleBinding giving settlement-agent get and patch on that one flag. auth can-i patch: yes.
SAY: "Now someone makes a mistake, the kind every real cluster collects. RBAC now says yes."
4. SHOW the third row: the same patch. Point at the policy name, agents-cannot-edit-their-own-authority, and DENIED. Read the end aloud: "Authority changes go through a reviewed commit, never a runtime decision by the agent."
SAY: "Each check assumes the last one failed. RBAC failed, on purpose, and the keystone held."
5. SHOW the fourth and fifth rows: the over-grant deleted (on every exit path, Ctrl-C included), and the flag still resolves assisted.
SAY, and credit William: "William has the line for this: we scripted the attempt. The platform scripts the response. The agent can never edit what constrains it."

IF ASKED "but Backstage can change the flag": yes, as Backstage's own narrow identity, which the policy doesn't match. People change authority through the reviewed path; the agent can't.

IF IT FAILS: "FAIL … is not Ready": Kyverno or stage 7 isn't up. "FAIL … over-grant is already applied": ./scripts/demo reset. "FAIL … not by the keystone": Kyverno didn't fire and RBAC did. Say so and move on.

[verify: Kyverno v1.19.1 (chart 3.9.1) still the latest stable before November. The policy is a ValidatingPolicy (policies.kyverno.io/v1), written in CEL; the legacy ClusterPolicy is deprecated since 1.19 (kyverno/kyverno#16868). William's OSFF demo used ClusterPolicy on v1.18.1.]

———

Step 5 · live · terminal. Prove.

1. DO: ./scripts/demo evidence. About a second. It reads this run's three claims back from Jaeger, and nothing older. The first claim's link is the approval's own trace: its northstar.review.decision span is where "approved by" and "after N s" come from.
2. SHOW the first claim, the one a human approved: the decision service sent it to a human. Rule settlement-agent.assisted.execute_limit, limit 0, autonomy level assisted. Outcome SETTLED, by reviewer-ui. Approved by the stage reviewer, after about twenty seconds. That number is the human wait, read off the reviewer's own span.
3. SHOW the second: PERMIT, under a different rule, settlement-agent.autonomous.execute_limit, limit 6,000. SETTLED by the agent. Approved by: none.
4. SHOW the third, the 6,200 claim: sent to a human, limit 6,000, still waiting, nothing moved. Approved by: none, yet.
SAY: "For each claim: who decided, the rule, who approved, how long the human took."
SAY: "Every line here is a span attribute, read back from Jaeger. Nothing is reconstructed."
Don't say "same rule, different amount" here: that's the longer evidence view in Act 4 (5,800 against 6,200 at one level), not this run.

IF IT FAILS: it waits for Jaeger for up to 90 seconds, then names the fields that never arrived. "FAIL no claims in this run yet": a reset ran between the claims and this. Say so and move on.

[verify: re-time at rehearsal; measured on the OpenSearch reader]

———

TIMING (measured): the commands take about 55 seconds in total; the rest is you talking. Step 1 waits 8 seconds on purpose (the drop). Steps 2 and 3 each pause about 15 seconds while every service's spans land in Jaeger; those notes say what to fill the pause with.

PRE-FLIGHT, done before the talk (runbook §4):
1. ./scripts/setup-kind.sh --stage 7 printed ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: SET. ./scripts/start-demo.sh is running in its own terminal.
2. Every pod Running, Kyverno's included, and the keystone policy Ready: kubectl get validatingpolicy agents-cannot-edit-their-own-authority.
3. Rehearse once: ./scripts/demo claim 5800 --expect awaiting_approval, then ./scripts/demo approve last. The claim exits non-zero unless it waits for a human.
4. The last thing you type before the audience arrives: ./scripts/demo reset. It sets the flag to assisted, removes any over-grant and clears the run's claims. It is safe at any time.
5. A terminal at the repo root, font large, about 100 columns wide.

Source: docs/demo-runbook.md §5 "The five-minute flow"; M7 design spec §7; scratchpad flow/*.txt and flow/timings.md (stage-7 run, 2026-10-12)
